summary.text: If primes \(p,q\) have different final digits, \(pq\le150\), and neither divides \(d\), then invertibility modulo \(pq\) makes one of the first \(pq\) terms divisible by both, a contradiction. Applying this to selected pairs successively forces \(2,5,3,7\mid d\), hence \(210\mid d\); the bound \(d\le2025\) then excludes both \(11\mid d\) and \(13\mid d\), while \(11\cdot13=143\le150\) gives the final contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let us call an integer greater than 1 lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same final decimal digit. We prove that there do not exist integers
\[
a\ge 2,\qquad 1\le d\le 2025
\]
for which all 150 integers
\[
a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
are lopsided.

We first establish the modular obstruction that will be used repeatedly.

**Modular obstruction.** Let \(p\) and \(q\) be primes whose final decimal digits differ. Suppose that
\[
pq\le 150,
\]
and that neither \(p\) nor \(q\) divides \(d\). Then the progression cannot have all of its first 150 terms lopsided.

Indeed, because \(p\) and \(q\) are prime and neither divides \(d\), we have
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Thus multiplication by \(d\) is a permutation of the residue classes modulo \(pq\). Consequently, the congruence
\[
a+id\equiv 0\pmod{pq}
\]
has a solution \(i\) modulo \(pq\). Choose its representative with
\[
0\le i<pq.
\]
Since \(pq\le150\), this index satisfies \(0\le i<150\). The corresponding term \(a+id\) is divisible by \(pq\), and hence by both \(p\) and \(q\). Also \(a+id\ge a\ge2\), so it is nonzero and these are genuine prime divisors of the term. Since \(p\) and \(q\) have different final digits, this term is not lopsided, a contradiction.

Equivalently, under the hypothesis that all 150 terms are lopsided, we have the following useful implication:

> For every pair of primes \(p,q\) with different final digits and \(pq\le150\), at least one of \(p,q\) must divide \(d\).

Assume now, for contradiction, that suitable \(a,d\) exist. We apply this implication in several stages.

### 1. First, \(2\mid d\)

Suppose instead that \(2\nmid d\). Apply the modular obstruction to each of the following pairs:
\[
(2,3),\ (2,5),\ (2,7),\ (2,11),\ (2,13).
\]
The two primes in each pair have distinct final digits. Their products are, respectively,
\[
6,10,14,22,26,
\]
all at most 150. Since \(2\nmid d\), the obstruction forces the other prime in each pair to divide \(d\). Thus
\[
3\mid d,\quad 5\mid d,\quad 7\mid d,\quad 11\mid d,\quad 13\mid d.
\]
These are distinct primes, so their product divides \(d\):
\[
3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=15015\mid d.
\]
Because \(d\ge1\), this implies \(d\ge15015\), contradicting \(d\le2025\). Therefore
\[
2\mid d.
\]

### 2. Next, \(5\mid d\)

Suppose that \(5\nmid d\). Use the prime pairs
\[
(3,5),\ (5,7),\ (5,11),\ (5,13).
\]
Their final digits differ, and their products are
\[
15,35,55,65,
\]
all at most 150. Since \(5\nmid d\), the obstruction forces
\[
3\mid d,\quad 7\mid d,\quad 11\mid d,\quad 13\mid d.
\]
Together with the already established divisibility \(2\mid d\), and using that these five primes are distinct, we obtain
\[
2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=6006\mid d.
\]
Hence \(d\ge6006\), again contradicting \(d\le2025\). Therefore
\[
5\mid d.
\]

### 3. Next, \(3\mid d\)

Suppose that \(3\nmid d\). Apply the obstruction to
\[
(3,7),\ (3,11),\ (3,17).
\]
The final digits in these pairs are respectively \(3\) and \(7\), \(3\) and \(1\), and \(3\) and \(7\), so they differ. The products are
\[
21,33,51,
\]
all at most 150. Since \(3\nmid d\), it follows that
\[
7\mid d,\quad 11\mid d,\quad 17\mid d.
\]
Combining this with \(2\mid d\) and \(5\mid d\), and again using pairwise coprimality of the distinct primes, gives
\[
2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot17=13090\mid d.
\]
Thus \(d\ge13090\), contrary to \(d\le2025\). We conclude that
\[
3\mid d.
\]

### 4. Next, \(7\mid d\)

Suppose that \(7\nmid d\). Consider the pairs
\[
(7,11),\ (7,13).
\]
Their final digits are \(7,1\) and \(7,3\), respectively, and their products are
\[
77,91,
\]
which are at most 150. The modular obstruction therefore forces
\[
11\mid d\quad\text{and}\quad13\mid d.
\]
Together with
\[
2\mid d,\qquad3\mid d,\qquad5\mid d,
\]
this yields
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11\cdot13=4290\mid d.
\]
It follows that \(d\ge4290\), contradicting \(d\le2025\). Hence
\[
7\mid d.
\]

We have now proved
\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210\mid d.
\]

### 5. The final contradiction

Neither 11 nor 13 can divide \(d\). Indeed, if \(11\mid d\), then, since \(\gcd(210,11)=1\),
\[
210\cdot11=2310\mid d,
\]
which would imply \(d\ge2310>2025\). Thus \(11\nmid d\). Similarly, if \(13\mid d\), then
\[
210\cdot13=2730\mid d,
\]
forcing \(d\ge2730>2025\). Thus \(13\nmid d\).

Finally apply the modular obstruction to the primes \(11\) and \(13\). Their final decimal digits are \(1\) and \(3\), which differ, and
\[
11\cdot13=143\le150.
\]
We have just shown that neither prime divides \(d\). Therefore there is an index \(i\) with
\[
0\le i<143\le150
\]
such that
\[
143\mid a+id.
\]
Hence both 11 and 13 divide \(a+id\). That term has prime divisors ending in the two different digits 1 and 3, so it is not lopsided. This contradicts the assumption that every one of the first 150 terms is lopsided.

Therefore no integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) can produce a 150-term arithmetic progression all of whose terms occur in A381159. This disproves the conjectured existence statement.
